mainTopic: How a person should accept Divine judgment: the contrast between a human king's justice and the justice of הקדוש ברוך הוא (רבי ירמיה בן אלעזר), leading into a teaching of רבי יהושע בן לוי.
overview: This amud opens with the last words of a פסוק from the previous teaching. רבי ירמיה בן אלעזר then contrasts a human king, who must gag a condemned man, with הקדוש ברוך הוא: the person judged by ה׳ stays silent, praises Him, and feels as if he is bringing a קרבן. רבי יהושע בן לוי's reading of 'עוברי בעמק הבכא' teaches that sinners in גיהנם admit ה׳ judged them fairly. The גמרא challenges this from ריש לקיש, who says the wicked never repent. It answers that ריש לקיש means the sinners of the nations, because he also teaches that the fire of גיהנם has no power over Jewish sinners. אברהם אבינו brings Jewish sinners out of גיהנם, and רב כהנא questions ריש לקיש's reading of 'הפושעים'. Next come the three entrances of גיהנם and its seven names, the reasons 'גיהנם' and 'תפתה' are not counted as names, and the possible entrances to גן עדן. Finally the גמרא returns to the משנה about the boards around a well. It explains 'tied, not untied' and 'one team enters and one leaves', and begins a ברייתא on a cow's size that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Closing words of the previous verse
steps.stepSummary: This amud begins with the final words of מיכה א:ו, which closed the previous teaching.
steps.simpleTranslation: "...for planting vines."
steps.whatsHappening: These are the last words of a פסוק that the גמרא began quoting on the previous amud. It finishes the proof for the teaching that came just before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The full verse says ה׳ will make שומרון into a field for planting vines. Even a punishment from ה׳ leaves behind something useful for the people living nearby. This is not a new step in the argument. It only completes the earlier proof.

keyTerms.meaning: plantings, places where things are planted

steps.confusionAlert: Do not treat this as the start of a new topic. It is the tail end of a verse quoted on the previous amud.

phrases.english: for planting vines."
phrases.notes: End of the quote from מיכה א:ו.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the prooftext of the teaching earlier.
steps.raayaObject: The previous teaching, that even ה׳'s punishment carries some benefit.

steps.title: A human king must gag the condemned man
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה בן אלעזר begins a comparison: a human government puts a hook in a condemned man's mouth so he cannot curse the king.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי ירמיה בן אלעזר said: Come and see that the way of flesh and blood is not like the way of הקדוש ברוך הוא. The way of flesh and blood: when a person is sentenced to death by the government, they put a hook into his mouth so that he will not curse the king.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה בן אלעזר starts a new comparison. This step describes only the human side. The Divine side comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person sentenced by a human king feels he was treated unfairly and is full of anger. So the government has to force him to be silent with a hook. His silence is forced on him from outside.

keyTerms.meaning: come and see, a phrase that opens a contrast
the way of flesh and blood, meaning human behavior
a death sentence from the government
a hook, used here as a gag

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar said:
Come and see
that not like the attribute of the Holy One, Blessed be He,
is the attribute of flesh and blood.
The attribute of flesh and blood:
when a person is sentenced to death by the government,
they place a hook into his mouth
so that he will not curse the king.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר: בֹּא וּרְאֵה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching by the same אמורא, introduced with ואמר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Under human justice, the condemned man must be gagged because he would curse the king.

steps.title: Before ה׳, the condemned man is silent on his own
steps.stepSummary: The other side of the comparison: a person judged by ה׳ accepts it in silence, as the פסוק says, "לך דומיה תהלה."
steps.simpleTranslation: The way of הקדוש ברוך הוא: when a person is sentenced to death by the מקום, he stays silent, as it says: "For You, silence is praise."
steps.whatsHappening: This step completes the comparison. Under ה׳'s judgment, the person is quiet by his own choice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the king, silence had to be forced with a hook. Here the silence comes from inside, because the person knows ה׳'s judgment is fair. The word דומיה (silence) in the פסוק is the proof.

keyTerms.meaning: the Omnipresent, a name for ה׳

phrases.english: The attribute of the Holy One, Blessed be He:
when a person is sentenced to death by the Omnipresent,
he is silent,
as it is stated: "For You, silence is praise,"
phrases.notes: תהלים ס״ה:ב

steps.triggerLanguage: מִדַּת הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, אָדָם מִתְחַיֵּיב הֲרִיגָה לַמָּקוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the contrast that step 2 opened.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person judged by ה׳ accepts it in silence, without being forced.

steps.title: He even praises ה׳ and feels he is offering a sacrifice
steps.stepSummary: Two more levels, each learned from the same פסוק: the person praises ה׳‎ ("תהלה"), and he feels as if he is bringing a קרבן ("ולך ישולם נדר").
steps.simpleTranslation: And more than that, he praises, as it says: "praise." And more than that, it seems to him as if he is offering a קרבן, as it says: "and to You the vow shall be paid."
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה בן אלעזר goes beyond silence. He adds two higher levels, each with its own proof from the same פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ולא עוד אלא pattern builds step by step. First comes silence, then praise, then the feeling of offering a קרבן. Each word of the פסוק teaches one level. The suffering is seen as a כפרה, just as a קרבן brings atonement.

keyTerms.meaning: and not only that, but also; signals a higher level

steps.whatToRemember: There are three levels in accepting ה׳'s judgment: silence, then praise, then feeling it is like a קרבן. All three come from תהלים ס״ה:ב. This is the opposite of the gagged prisoner of a human king.

phrases.english: And not only that, but he praises,
as it is stated: "praise."
And not only that, but it seems to him
as though he is offering a sacrifice,
as it is stated: "And to You the vow shall be paid."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds higher levels beyond the silence of step 3, using the rest of the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person judged by ה׳ praises Him and sees his suffering as a קרבן that brings atonement.

steps.title: Linking to רבי יהושע בן לוי's verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says this idea matches a statement of רבי יהושע בן לוי, who asks what the פסוק "עוברי בעמק הבכא" means.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what רבי יהושע בן לוי said: What is the meaning of what is written: "Those who pass through the valley of weeping make it a spring; also the early rain covers it with blessings"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move. It connects the idea to רבי יהושע בן לוי and quotes his פסוק, but the explanation comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: הַיְינוּ דְּאָמַר tells us that רבי יהושע בן לוי's teaching expresses the same idea of accepting suffering. The question מאי דכתיב asks for the meaning of a פסוק. Steps 6-7 give the answer.

keyTerms.meaning: this is what [so-and-so] said; links two teachings
what is the meaning of what is written

steps.confusionAlert: Do not look here for the explanation. Steps 6-7 answer this question.

phrases.aramaic: הַיְינוּ דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי:
phrases.english: This is what Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
What is the meaning of that which is written:
"Those who pass through the valley of weeping
make it a spring;
also the early rain covers it with blessings"?
phrases.notes: תהלים פ״ד:ז

steps.triggerLanguage: הַיְינוּ דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי: מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Connects the idea of accepting Divine judgment to another אמורא's reading of a פסוק.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of תהלים פ״ד:ז, "עוברי בעמק הבכא."
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Answered in steps 6-7. רבי יהושע בן לוי explains each word: the sinners are punished in a deep גיהנם, they weep, and they declare that ה׳'s judgment is fair.

steps.title: Explaining the words of the verse: who the sinners are and how they are punished
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי explains the first words of the פסוק one by one. They describe people who go against ה׳'s will, who are punished in a deep גיהנם, and who cry rivers of tears.
steps.simpleTranslation: "עוברי" means people who go against what ה׳ wants. "עמק" means גיהנם is made deep for them. "הבכא" means they cry, and their tears flow like a spring that reaches down to the depths of the earth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now answers the question from the last step. It explains what each word of "עוברי בעמק הבכא" means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word is read by its sound. עוברי sounds like עוברין, people who cross a line. עמק sounds like מעמיקין, making something deep. בכא sounds like בוכין, crying. This first half describes the sin, the punishment, and the pain. The next step adds how the sinners react.

keyTerms.meaning: The place where the wicked are punished
The deep foundations or pits under the earth

phrases.english: "Those who pass through": these are people

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁעוֹבְרִין עַל רְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא.
phrases.english: who go against the will of the Holy One, Blessed be He.
phrases.notes: The word עוברי is being read as עוברין: people who cross over ה׳'s will.

phrases.english: "Valley": Gehenna is made deep for them.
phrases.notes: The word עמק, valley, is being read like מעמיקין, making deep.

phrases.english: "Of weeping": they cry and shed tears
like a spring that flows down to the foundations of the earth.
phrases.notes: This ties in to the words "מעין ישיתוהו" in the same פסוק.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״עוֹבְרֵי״ — אֵלּוּ בְּנֵי אָדָם שֶׁעוֹבְרִין עַל רְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question "מאי דכתיב עוברי בעמק הבכא" from step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The first words of the פסוק describe sinners who are punished in a deep גיהנם and cry heavily.

steps.title: The sinners admit that ה׳ judged them fairly
steps.stepSummary: The end of the פסוק teaches that the sinners in גיהנם accept their punishment. They tell ה׳ that His judgment was right.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Moreover, the early rain covers it with blessings" means that they admit the judgment is fair. They say to ה׳: Master of the world, You judged well. You found people innocent fairly, You found people guilty fairly, and You were right to make גיהנם for the wicked and גן עדן for the righteous.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the דרשה. This is the part that matches what רבי ירמיה בן אלעזר taught: a person judged by ה׳ accepts it and even praises Him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is why רבי יהושע בן לוי's teaching was brought here. Even sinners who are suffering in גיהנם say "You judged well." That is the same idea as "לך דומיה תהלה": you accept ה׳'s judgment, and you even praise Him.

keyTerms.meaning: They accept that the judgment against them is fair (צידוק הדין)
You found innocent / You found guilty
The place of reward for the righteous

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יהושע בן לוי, even sinners in גיהנם end up saying that ה׳'s judgment is fair. This is the link to רבי ירמיה בן אלעזר's teaching.

phrases.english: "Moreover, the early rain covers it with blessings":
they accept that the judgment against them is fair,
and they say before Him: Master of the Universe,

phrases.aramaic: יָפֶה דַּנְתָּ, יָפֶה זִכֵּיתָ, יָפֶה חִיַּיבְתָּ,
phrases.english: You judged well, You acquitted well, You condemned well,
and You did well to prepare Gehenna for the wicked
and the Garden of Eden for the righteous.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״גַּם בְּרָכוֹת יַעְטֶה מוֹרֶה״ — שֶׁמַּצְדִּיקִין עֲלֵיהֶם אֶת הַדִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the reading of the פסוק and shows how it matches רבי ירמיה בן אלעזר.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The sinners in גיהנם say that ה׳'s judgment is fair and they praise it.

steps.title: Challenge: ריש לקיש says the wicked never repent
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how this can be true. ריש לקיש taught that the wicked do not repent even at the doorway of גיהנם. He learns this from a פסוק that says they "keep on rebelling."
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that really so? Didn't ריש לקיש say that the wicked do not do תשובה even at the entrance to גיהנם? The פסוק says, "They will go out and see the bodies of the people who rebel against Me." It does not say "who rebelled." It says "who rebel," which means they keep on rebelling forever.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the teaching it just learned. If the wicked admit that ה׳ is right, how can ריש לקיש say they never stop rebelling?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Admitting that ה׳'s judgment is fair is a kind of turning back to Him. ריש לקיש reads the present tense "הפושעים" to mean they never stop sinning, even after they are punished. These two teachings seem to say opposite things.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי שמעון בן לקיש and ריש לקיש are the same person. ריש לקיש is just the short form of his name.

phrases.english: Is that so?!
But didn't Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish say:

phrases.aramaic: רְשָׁעִים אֲפִילּוּ עַל פִּתְחוֹ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם
phrases.english: The wicked, even at the entrance to Gehenna,
do not repent,
as it is said: "And they shall go out and look at the corpses of the men
who rebel against Me, etc."
phrases.notes: ישעיה סו:כד

phrases.english: It does not say "who rebelled," but rather "who rebel":
they go on rebelling forever!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי?! וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the claim from step 7 that sinners in גיהנם accept ה׳'s judgment.
steps.kashyaTarget: The teaching that sinners in גיהנם say ה׳'s judgment is fair.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ריש לקיש reads the present tense "הפושעים" to mean the wicked never stop rebelling, even at גיהנם. That clashes with the idea that they admit ה׳ is right.

steps.title: Answer: Jewish sinners versus sinners of the nations
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the two teachings are about two different groups. The sinners who accept the judgment are Jewish sinners. The sinners who never repent are from the nations of the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not a problem. One teaching is about the sinners of ישראל. The other teaching is about the sinners of the nations of the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the contradiction by saying each teaching is talking about a different group of people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Jewish sinners in גיהנם admit that ה׳ was right, as רבי יהושע בן לוי taught. ריש לקיש's "they keep rebelling" is about the sinners of the nations. So both teachings are true.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult (a standard opening for an answer)

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this one is about the sinners of Israel,
phrases.notes: This refers to רבי יהושע בן לוי: they accept the judgment.

phrases.english: that one is about the sinners of the nations of the world.
phrases.notes: This refers to ריש לקיש: they never repent.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא — בְּפוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, הָא — בְּפוֹשְׁעֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each teaching is about a different group.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both teachings seemed to talk about all the wicked, so they seemed to contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Jewish sinners accept the judgment. Sinners of the nations keep on rebelling.

steps.title: Support for the answer from another statement of ריש לקיש
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says this answer makes sense. If ריש לקיש meant Jewish sinners too, he would contradict himself. Elsewhere he says the fire of גיהנם has no power over Jewish sinners, learned by a קל וחומר from the מזבח הזהב.
steps.simpleTranslation: It also makes sense to say this. Otherwise ריש לקיש would contradict ריש לקיש. For ריש לקיש said: the fire of גיהנם has no power over the sinners of ישראל. This is learned by a קל וחומר from the golden מזבח.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for its answer. It quotes the start of a second teaching of ריש לקיש, and it is setting up the explanation of that קל וחומר, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If ריש לקיש's "they never repent" included Jewish sinners, it would clash with his own teaching that גיהנם's fire does not rule over them. So his "never repent" teaching must be about the nations. This supports the answer from step 9.

keyTerms.meaning: So too it is logical (introduces support)
An argument from a lighter case to a stronger one
The golden altar in the בית המקדש

steps.whatToRemember: The final answer is that Jewish sinners accept ה׳'s judgment and are not ruled by the fire of גיהנם, while ריש לקיש's "never repent" is about the sinners of the nations.
steps.confusionAlert: The קל וחומר from the מזבח הזהב is only named here. Steps 11-12 explain it.

phrases.english: So too it is reasonable,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִם כֵּן קַשְׁיָא דְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אַדְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ.
phrases.english: for if not so, Reish Lakish would contradict Reish Lakish.
phrases.notes: Meaning: if we do not split the cases this way.

phrases.english: As Reish Lakish said:

phrases.aramaic: פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵין אוּר גֵּיהִנָּם שׁוֹלֶטֶת בָּהֶן,
phrases.english: The fire of Gehenna has no power over the sinners of Israel,
as learned by a kal vachomer from the golden altar.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי נָמֵי מִסְתַּבְּרָא, דְּאִם כֵּן קַשְׁיָא דְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אַדְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 9 by showing it is needed to avoid ריש לקיש contradicting himself.
steps.raayaObject: The answer that ריש לקיש's "they never repent" is about the sinners of the nations.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ריש לקיש's own teaching that the fire of גיהנם has no power over the sinners of ישראל (a קל וחומר from the מזבח הזהב).

steps.title: The golden altar never burned, and Jewish sinners are full of מצוות
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש's קל וחומר begins. The thin gold covering of the מזבח הזהב survived fire for many years. Jewish sinners are far 'thicker' with מצוות, like a pomegranate full of seeds.
steps.simpleTranslation: Look at the golden altar. It had only a thin layer of gold, as thin as a gold coin, and it stood for many years without the fire burning it. Now look at the sinners of Israel. They are full of מצוות like a pomegranate, as the פסוק says: 'Like a split pomegranate is your temple.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now spells out the קל וחומר that ריש לקיש uses to show that the fire of גיהנם cannot hurt Jewish sinners. This step sets up both sides of the comparison. The conclusion comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'small' case is the מזבח הזהב: its gold layer was very thin, yet fire never melted it. The 'big' case is פושעי ישראל: even they are packed with מצוות like a pomegranate is packed with seeds. If a thin layer of gold resisted fire, a thick layer of מצוות should certainly protect a person.

keyTerms.meaning: The golden altar inside the היכל, where the קטורת was burned
A gold coin; used here as a measure of how thin the gold was
Pomegranate, famous for being full of seeds
The fire had power over it

phrases.english: Just as the golden altar,
phrases.notes: Opens the 'small' side of the קל וחומר.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין עָלָיו אֶלָּא כְּעוֹבִי דִּינַר זָהָב,
phrases.english: which had on it only gold as thick as a gold dinar,
stood for many years
and the fire did not have power over it.
phrases.notes: The gold never melted, even though burning coals were placed on it twice every day for the קטורת.

phrases.english: the sinners of Israel,
phrases.notes: Opens the 'big' side of the קל וחומר.

phrases.english: who are full of מצוות like a pomegranate,
as it says: 'Like a split pomegranate is your temple,'
phrases.notes: שיר השירים ו:ז. The next step explains how this פסוק is read.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the content of the קל וחומר that step 10 mentioned.
steps.raayaObject: That the fire of גיהנם has no power over Jewish sinners
steps.raayaSupportSource: The מזבח הזהב, whose thin gold covering survived fire for many years, together with the pomegranate פסוק

steps.title: Even the 'empty' ones are full of מצוות, so how much more so
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש rereads 'רקתך' as 'ריקתיך', meaning 'your empty ones'. Even the emptiest Jews are full of מצוות, so the קל וחומר is complete.
steps.simpleTranslation: And ריש לקיש said: Don't read the word as 'רַקָּתֵךְ' (your temple). Read it as 'רֵיקָתֵיךְ' (your empty ones). This teaches that even the empty people among you are full of מצוות like a pomegranate. So it is all the more true that the fire cannot touch them.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש shows from the pomegranate פסוק that even sinners are full of מצוות. He then closes the קל וחומר with 'על אחת כמה וכמה'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plain פסוק talks about a 'temple' (part of the head). With an אל תיקרי, ריש לקיש rereads it as 'empty ones', which means the sinners. That proves the 'big' side of the comparison. The ending phrase completes the logic: if fire spared a thin layer of gold, it will surely spare people this full of מצוות.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Do not read it as…': a way of drawing a lesson by rereading a word with different vowels
Empty ones; people who seem to have no good deeds
'How much more so': the closing phrase of a קל וחומר

steps.whatToRemember: ריש לקיש teaches that the fire of גיהנם cannot hurt Jewish sinners. His proof: the gold on the מזבח הזהב did not melt, and even the 'empty' Jews are full of מצוות like a pomegranate.
steps.confusionAlert: 'אל תיקרי' does not change the text of the פסוק. It adds a second layer of meaning on top of the plain reading.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said:
Do not read it as 'rakatech' (your temple),
but as 'reikateich' (your empty ones),
meaning that even the empty ones among you
are full of מצוות like a pomegranate.
So how much more so (will the fire not have power over them).
phrases.notes: This closes the קל וחומר that began with 'מה מזבח הזהב' in step 11.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proves the 'full of מצוות' side of the comparison and completes the קל וחומר.
steps.raayaObject: That even Jewish sinners are full of מצוות, so the fire cannot touch them
steps.raayaSupportSource: The rereading of 'רקתך' as 'ריקתיך' in שיר השירים ו:ז

steps.title: But a verse says sinners pass through the valley of weeping
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if fire cannot touch Jewish sinners, what about the פסוק 'עוברי בעמק הבכא'? Earlier it was explained as Jewish sinners crying in גיהנם.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about the פסוק that says: 'Those who pass through the valley of weeping'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a problem with what it just proved. Earlier (step 6), this פסוק was explained as describing sinners going down into גיהנם and crying there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע בן לוי read 'עוברי בעמק הבכא' as Jewish sinners being punished in גיהנם. That clashes with ריש לקיש's rule that the fire has no power over Jewish sinners. The גמרא needs a way to fit both together.

keyTerms.meaning: 'But what about that which is written…': opens a challenge from a פסוק
'Those who pass through the valley of weeping' (תהלים פד:ז)

phrases.english: But that which is written:
'Those who pass through the valley of weeping' — (what does it mean)?
phrases.notes: This is the same פסוק that was explained in step 6.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the conclusion of step 12 using the פסוק from step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's rule that the fire of גיהנם has no power over Jewish sinners
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק, as explained in step 6, describes Jewish sinners in גיהנם. So it seems they are punished there after all.

steps.title: אברהם אבינו lifts his children out, except one kind of sinner
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק describes sinners who deserve גיהנם. אברהם אבינו comes and brings them up. The exception is a Jew who lived with a non-Jewish woman: his ברית מילה is covered, so אברהם does not recognize him.
steps.simpleTranslation: That פסוק is about people who are sentenced to גיהנם at that moment. But אברהם אבינו comes, lifts them up, and takes them in. The exception is a Jew who was with a non-Jewish woman. His foreskin is drawn back over, and אברהם does not recognize him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. Jewish sinners are sentenced to גיהנם, but they do not stay there, because אברהם אבינו rescues them. The גמרא then names one sinner he does not rescue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Passing through the valley of weeping' describes the sentence the sinners deserve. It does not mean the fire actually rules over them, because אברהם brings them up. The one exception is someone who damaged the sign of the ברית with an act of אישות with a non-Jew. Since his מילה is hidden, אברהם does not know him as his own.

keyTerms.meaning: His foreskin is drawn back over, so his מילה is covered

steps.whatToRemember: Jewish sinners may be sentenced to גיהנם, but אברהם אבינו brings them out. The only exception is one who 'erased' his ברית by being with a non-Jewish woman.
steps.confusionAlert: The answer does not say Jewish sinners are never sentenced. It says they are sentenced, but אברהם pulls them out, so the fire never gets to rule over them.

phrases.english: That refers to those who are sentenced to Gehinnom at that moment,
and Avraham Avinu comes
and brings them up and receives them.
Except for a Jew who had relations with a non-Jewish woman,
whose foreskin is drawn back over,
and (Avraham) does not recognize him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the פסוק: it describes the sentence the sinners deserve, not their actual stay in the fire
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק means Jewish sinners actually suffer in the fire of גיהנם.
steps.terutzMaskana: They are sentenced, but אברהם אבינו brings them out. Only one who covered his מילה by being with a non-Jew stays.

steps.title: רב כהנא: does 'He who brings out' mean He is still doing it?
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא attacks ריש לקיש's reading that 'הפושעים' means 'those who keep on rebelling'. By that logic, 'המוציא' and 'המעלה' would have to mean ה׳ is still taking us out of מצרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא challenged this. Now that you say 'those who rebel' means 'those who keep on rebelling', then in the verses that say 'He who brings out' and 'He who raises up', does that mean ה׳ is still raising us up and still bringing us out?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא goes back to ריש לקיש's proof from step 8 and challenges how ריש לקיש read the word 'הפושעים'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש took the present-tense form 'הפושעים' to mean the rebelling never stops, even at the doorway of גיהנם. רב כהנא points out that the same kind of word is used for ה׳ taking us out of מצרים. Nobody would say that event is still going on, so the grammatical form alone proves nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: 'If so, then…': introduces an absurd result of someone's logic
'He who brings out' and 'He who raises up': describing ה׳ taking us out of מצרים

phrases.english: Rav Kahana strongly objected to this:
Now that you say 'those who rebel'
means those who keep on rebelling,
phrases.notes: This is ריש לקיש's reading from step 8.

phrases.english: then, where it is written
'He who brings out' and 'He who raises up',
does it mean He is still raising up and bringing out?!
phrases.notes: A rhetorical question: obviously not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to ריש לקיש's proof from step 8 and attacks it.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's reading that 'הפושעים' means 'those who keep on rebelling'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same present-tense form is used in 'המוציא' and 'המעלה', which clearly describe something that already happened. So the form cannot prove the rebelling is ongoing.

steps.title: So 'those who rebel' means those who already rebelled
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא concludes: 'המוציא' means 'who brought out', so 'הפושעים' can just mean 'who rebelled' in the past. This knocks out ריש לקיש's proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it must mean 'He who raised up and brought out' in the past. So here too, it means 'those who rebelled' in the past.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא finishes his challenge. 'הפושעים' simply describes people who sinned before. It does not describe people who keep sinning even at the door of גיהנם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the word can describe a past action, the פסוק no longer proves that the wicked never do תשובה at the doorway of גיהנם. That removes the source for ריש לקיש's teaching in step 8.

keyTerms.meaning: Who (already) raised up and brought out

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how the גמרא tests a proof built on a word's grammar: it checks whether the same form is used elsewhere in a way that cannot fit the proof.

phrases.english: Rather, it means He who raised up and brought out (in the past);
here too, it means those who (already) rebelled.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב כהנא's challenge by stating what follows from it.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects ריש לקיש's proof from 'הפושעים' that the wicked never repent at the doorway of גיהנם
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The present-tense form can describe a past action, as 'המוציא' and 'המעלה' show.

steps.title: גיהנם has three entrances
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה בר אלעזר teaches that גיהנם has three entrances: one in the מדבר, one in the sea, and one in ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי ירמיה בר אלעזר said: גיהנם has three entrances. One is in the מדבר, one is in the sea, and one is in ירושלים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new teaching about גיהנם: it has three entrances. The proofs for each location come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new statement, not part of the debate before it. It lists three places, and the גמרא will now bring a פסוק for each one, starting with the מדבר.

keyTerms.meaning: The place where the wicked are punished

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yirmeya bar Elazar said:
Gehinnom has three entrances:
one in the wilderness, one in the sea,
and one in Jerusalem.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about גיהנם, separate from the debate that came before.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גיהנם has three entrances: in the מדבר, in the sea, and in ירושלים.

steps.title: The entrance in the מדבר: קורח went down alive
steps.stepSummary: The source for the entrance in the מדבר is קורח and his group, who went down alive into the 'שאול'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The entrance in the מדבר: as it is written about קורח and his group: 'And they and all that was theirs went down alive into שאול.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק for the first of the three entrances, the one in the מדבר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: קורח and his group were swallowed by the ground in the מדבר and went down 'שאולה', which is a name for גיהנם. So there must be an opening to גיהנם in the מדבר.

keyTerms.meaning: Into שאול; a name for גיהנם

phrases.english: In the wilderness, as it is written:
'And they and all that was theirs went down
phrases.notes: במדבר טז:לג, about קורח and his group.

phrases.english: alive into the pit.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the first entrance listed in step 17.
steps.raayaObject: That גיהנם has an entrance in the מדבר
steps.raayaSupportSource: במדבר טז:לג: קורח and his group went down alive into שאול

steps.title: Proof for the entrance in the sea
steps.stepSummary: The entrance to גיהנם in the sea is learned from יונה, who cried out to ה׳ 'from the belly of שאול' while inside the fish in the sea.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the sea: as it is written, 'From the belly of שאול I cried out, and You heard my voice.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a source for the second of the three entrances, the one in the sea.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יונה was inside a fish in the middle of the sea, yet he said he was calling out 'from the belly of שאול.' Since שאול is a name for גיהנם, this shows there is an opening to גיהנם in the sea. It follows the same method as the previous step, where קורח going down into 'שאול' proved an entrance in the מדבר.

keyTerms.meaning: From the belly of שאול (a name for גיהנם)

phrases.english: In the sea, as it is written:
'From the belly of She'ol I cried out,
phrases.notes: יונה 2:3, said by יונה from inside the fish

phrases.english: You heard my voice.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of proofs for the three entrances. The previous step proved the entrance in the מדבר, and this step proves the one in the sea.
steps.raayaObject: רבי ירמיה בר אלעזר's claim that one entrance to גיהנם is in the sea
steps.raayaSupportSource: יונה 2:3: 'מִבֶּטֶן שְׁאוֹל שִׁוַּעְתִּי', said from inside the fish in the sea

steps.title: Proof for the entrance in ירושלים
steps.stepSummary: The entrance in ירושלים is learned from ישעיהו, who speaks of ה׳'s 'fire in ציון' and 'furnace in ירושלים.' The school of רבי ישמעאל explains that the fire is גיהנם and the furnace is its entrance.
steps.simpleTranslation: In ירושלים: as it is written, 'Says ה׳, Whose fire is in ציון and Whose furnace is in ירושלים.' And the school of רבי ישמעאל taught: 'Whose fire is in ציון' means גיהנם. 'Whose furnace is in ירושלים' means the entrance to גיהנם.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves the third entrance, the one in ירושלים, using a פסוק and a ברייתא that explains it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק alone only mentions a 'fire' and a 'furnace.' The ברייתא from the school of רבי ישמעאל turns this into a proof: the fire is גיהנם itself, and the furnace in ירושלים is its opening. A furnace has an opening where the fire is reached, so it fits the idea of an entrance.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in the school of רבי ישמעאל (a ברייתא)

steps.whatToRemember: The three entrances to גיהנם are in the מדבר (קורח), in the sea (יונה), and in ירושלים (ישעיהו's 'furnace').

phrases.english: In Jerusalem, as it is written:
'Says ה׳, Whose fire is in Zion,
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 31:9

phrases.english: and Whose furnace is in Jerusalem.'
And the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
'Whose fire is in Zion': this is Gehinnom.

phrases.aramaic: ״וְתַנּוּר לוֹ בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם״ — זוֹ פִּתְחָהּ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם.
phrases.english: 'And Whose furnace is in Jerusalem': this is the entrance of Gehinnom.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the third and final proof for רבי ירמיה בר אלעזר's three entrances.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that one entrance to גיהנם is in ירושלים
steps.raayaSupportSource: ישעיהו 31:9, as explained by the ברייתא of the school of רבי ישמעאל

steps.title: Is there a fourth entrance between two date palms?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether there are really only three entrances. Another teaching says there are two date palms in גיא בן הנום with smoke rising between them, and that this spot is 'the entrance of גיהנם.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Are there no more? But רבי מריון said in the name of רבי יהושע בן לוי (some say רבה בר מריון taught it in the school of רבי יוחנן בן זכאי): There are two date palms in גיא בן הנום, and smoke rises from between them. These are the palms we learned about: 'The palms of הר הברזל are kosher.' And this is the entrance of גיהנם!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the claim of only three entrances. It points to a teaching that seems to describe another entrance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ירמיה בר אלעזר counted exactly three entrances. A different teaching calls the place between two smoking palms in גיא בן הנום 'the entrance of גיהנם.' The question is whether this is a fourth entrance he left out. These palms are the same ones mentioned in the teaching that the palms of הר הברזל are kosher for a לולב.

keyTerms.meaning: Is there no more? (Is the list really complete?)
The valley of בן הנום, next to ירושלים

steps.confusionAlert: The line about the palms of הר הברזל being kosher (for a לולב) is not the main point here. It only identifies which palms are meant. The real challenge is the last phrase: 'this is the entrance of גיהנם.'

phrases.english: And are there no more?
But didn't Rabbi Maryon say
in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ תָּנָא רַבָּה בַּר מָרִיּוֹן
phrases.english: and some say Rabbah bar Maryon taught it
in the name of the school of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai:

phrases.aramaic: שְׁתֵּי תְמָרוֹת יֵשׁ בְּגֵי בֶּן הִנּוֹם
phrases.english: There are two date palms in the valley of ben Hinnom
and smoke rises from between them.
And this is what we learned:
'The palms of Har HaBarzel are kosher' (for a lulav),
and this is the entrance of Gehinnom!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the three entrances are proven, the גמרא tests whether the count of three is complete.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ירמיה בר אלעזר's statement that גיהנם has exactly three entrances
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another teaching names the smoking spot between two palms in גיא בן הנום as 'the entrance of גיהנם.' That seems to be a fourth entrance missing from the list of three.

steps.title: The palms are the ירושלים entrance
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the entrance between the palms may simply be the same entrance as the one in ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps this is the one in ירושלים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The palm-tree entrance is not a new, fourth entrance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: גיא בן הנום is right next to ירושלים. So the entrance between the two palms is just a more exact description of where the ירושלים entrance is. The count of three entrances stays as it was.

phrases.english: Perhaps this is the one of Jerusalem.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the challenge from the previous step.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identification: the two sources describe the same entrance
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The palm-tree entrance in גיא בן הנום is a fourth entrance that the list of three left out.
steps.terutzMaskana: The palm-tree entrance is the same as the ירושלים entrance, so there are still only three.

steps.title: The seven names of גיהנם
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי teaches that גיהנם has seven names: שאול, אבדון, באר שחת, בור שאון, טיט היון, צלמות, and ארץ התחתית.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן לוי said: גיהנם has seven names, and these are they: שאול, אבדון, באר שחת, בור שאון, טיט היון, צלמות, and ארץ התחתית.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching from רבי יהושע בן לוי that lists the seven names of גיהנם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new statement, not a reply to the previous discussion. It fits here because the earlier proofs already relied on 'שאול' being a name for גיהנם. Six of the names come from a פסוק, and the seventh (ארץ התחתית) comes from tradition. Each describes גיהנם in a different way, such as destruction, a pit, mud, or deep darkness.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:

phrases.aramaic: שִׁבְעָה שֵׁמוֹת יֵשׁ לְגֵיהִנָּם, וְאֵלּוּ הֵן:
phrases.english: Gehinnom has seven names, and these are they:
She'ol, Avadon, Be'er Shachat,
Bor Sha'on, Tit HaYaven,
Tzalmavet, and Eretz HaTachtit (the lowest land).

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי: שִׁבְעָה שֵׁמוֹת יֵשׁ לְגֵיהִנָּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic connected to the discussion of גיהנם. It is related to the earlier steps but does not answer them.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גיהנם has seven names: שאול, אבדון, באר שחת, בור שאון, טיט היון, צלמות, and ארץ התחתית.

steps.title: A פסוק for each of the seven names of גיהנם
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a פסוק for six of the seven names of גיהנם. For the seventh name, ארץ התחתית, it says the source is a received tradition.
steps.simpleTranslation: שאול: as it says, 'From the belly of שאול I cried out, You heard my voice.' אבדון: as it says, 'Will Your kindness be told in the grave, Your faithfulness in אבדון?' באר שחת: as it says, 'You will not leave my soul to שאול, You will not let Your pious one see שחת.' בור שאון and טיט היון: as it says, 'He lifted me up from the בור שאון, from the טיט היון.' צלמות: as it says, 'Those who sit in darkness and צלמות.' ארץ התחתית: this is known by tradition.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back over the seven names that רבי יהושע בן לוי just listed and shows where in תנ״ך each one comes from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each name is tied to a פסוק in which that word describes a place of death or destruction. בור שאון and טיט היון share one פסוק, so they are proven together. ארץ התחתית has no verse, so the גמרא says it is 'גמרא', meaning a tradition passed down.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written (introduces a פסוק as the source)
The netherworld; the first name of גיהנם
The shadow of death; a name of גיהנם
It is a received tradition (here it does not mean the Talmud)

steps.confusionAlert: The phrase 'גמרא הוא' here does not mean 'it is in the Talmud.' It means 'it is a tradition we received,' with no פסוק as the source.

phrases.english: She'ol, as it is written:
"From the belly of She'ol I cried out; You heard my voice" (Yonah 2:3).
phrases.notes: יונה said this from inside the fish. The same פסוק came up in step 19.

phrases.english: Avadon, as it is written:
"Will Your kindness be told in the grave,
Your faithfulness in Avadon (destruction)?" (Tehillim 88:12).
Be'er Shachat, as it is written:
"For You will not abandon my soul to She'ol,
You will not let Your pious one see the pit (shachat)" (Tehillim 16:10).
And Bor Sha'on and Tit HaYaven, as it is written:
"He brought me up from the roaring pit, from the miry clay" (Tehillim 40:3).
phrases.notes: One verse is the source for two names.

phrases.english: And Tzalmaves, as it is written:
"Those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death" (Tehillim 107:10).
And Eretz HaTachtis (the lowest land): it is a tradition.
phrases.notes: There's no פסוק for this name; it was simply handed down.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source verses for the seven names listed in step 23.
steps.raayaObject: That each of the seven names really is a name of גיהנם.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Verses from יונה and תהלים, plus a tradition for ארץ התחתית.

steps.title: Why isn't 'גיהנם' itself on the list?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the count of seven. Isn't 'גיהנם' itself also a name?
steps.simpleTranslation: Are there no more names? But there is the name 'גיהנם'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the claim that there are only seven names. The most famous name of all, 'גיהנם,' is missing from the list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע בן לוי gave an exact number, seven. If 'גיהנם' is also a name, the count should be eight. So the challenge targets the precision of the list.

keyTerms.meaning: And is there no more? (questions whether a list is complete)
But there is! (points to a missing item)

phrases.english: And there are no more?
But there is the name "Gehinnom"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the completeness of the seven-name list from steps 23-24.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that גיהנם has exactly seven names.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The well-known name 'גיהנם' is not among the seven, so the list seems incomplete.

steps.title: גיהנם is a description, not a name
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'גיהנם' describes the place rather than naming it. It is a deep valley, and people go down into it because of empty, wasted deeds.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a valley as deep as the valley of בן הנום, into which everyone goes down because of empty (חנם) deeds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. 'גיהנם' is not a separate name; it is a description built from the words גיא (valley) and הנם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: גיא means a deep valley, like the valley of בן הנום. הנם is read as if it were חנם, meaning 'for nothing,' so it refers to people who fall in because of empty, worthless deeds. Since the word only describes the place, it is not counted as a name.

keyTerms.meaning: Because of empty deeds (הנם read like חנם, 'for nothing')

phrases.english: A valley that is deep (like the valley of Hinnom),
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the words in round brackets, which compare the valley's depth to the valley of בן הנום.

phrases.english: into which everyone goes down
because of empty, worthless deeds.
phrases.notes: A wordplay: הנם is read like חנם, meaning 'for nothing.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation: the word is a description, not a proper name.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'גיהנם' is an eighth name that the list left out.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'גיהנם' only describes the place (a deep valley, entered because of empty deeds), so the count of seven stands.

steps.title: Why isn't 'תפתה' on the list?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא raises a second challenge. 'תפתה' appears in a פסוק as a name for גיהנם, so why isn't it on the list?
steps.simpleTranslation: But there is also the name 'תפתה,' as it says, 'For תפתה has been prepared from long ago.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the count of seven again. This time it points to the word 'תפתה,' which ישעיהו uses for גיהנם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This challenge is stronger than the first, because this name actually appears in a פסוק. That is the same kind of source the גמרא used to prove the other names. So it seems 'תפתה' should be counted too.

keyTerms.meaning: Tofteh; a term for גיהנם in ישעיהו

phrases.english: But there is also "Tofteh," as it is written:
"For Tofteh has been prepared from long ago" (Yeshayahu 30:33).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge of the same kind as step 25.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that גיהנם has exactly seven names.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק calls גיהנם 'תפתה,' so it seems to be a missing eighth name.

steps.title: תפתה describes who falls there
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'תפתה' is also a description. It describes whoever lets himself be seduced (מתפתה) by his יצר הרע.
steps.simpleTranslation: That word means that whoever is seduced by his יצר will fall there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the second challenge the same way as the first. 'תפתה' is a description, not a name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word תפתה is linked to מתפתה, meaning 'seduced.' It describes who ends up there, not what the place is called. So the count of seven names stays the same.
steps.whatToRemember: There are seven true names of גיהנם. 'גיהנם' and 'תפתה' are descriptions: a deep valley people fall into because of empty deeds, and the place where whoever is seduced by his יצר falls.

phrases.english: That means: anyone who lets himself be seduced by his inclination
will fall there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation through wordplay: the term is a description, not a name.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'תפתה' is an eighth name of גיהנם.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'תפתה' describes those who are seduced by their יצר and fall there, so it is not counted as a name.

steps.title: Where the entrance to גן עדן would be
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש teaches where the entrance to גן עדן is, depending on where גן עדן is located. Each possible entrance is a very fertile place.
steps.simpleTranslation: About גן עדן: ריש לקיש said, if it is in ארץ ישראל, its entrance is בית שאן. If it is in Arabia, its entrance is בית גרם. If it is between the rivers, its entrance is דומסקנין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא has finished with גיהנם and now turns to the opposite place, גן עדן. ריש לקיש names its entrance under three possible locations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא discussed the entrances to גיהנם; now it discusses the entrance to גן עדן. ריש לקיש is not sure where גן עדן is, so he gives a 'pathway' for each possible region. Each place he names is known for its rich, lush land, which hints at the beauty of גן עדן.

keyTerms.meaning: Between the rivers (the region of בבל)

phrases.english: The Garden of Eden:
phrases.notes: A heading that opens the new topic.

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said:
If it is in Eretz Yisrael,
Beis She'an is its entrance;
and if in Arabia, Beis Gerem is its entrance;
and if it is between the rivers,
Dumaskenin is its entrance.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the entrances of גיהנם to the entrance of גן עדן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The entrance to גן עדן is בית שאן, בית גרם, or דומסקנין, depending on whether גן עדן is in ארץ ישראל, Arabia, or between the rivers.

steps.title: אביי and רבא praise the fruits of בבל
steps.stepSummary: In בבל, אביי praised the fruit of the right bank of the river, and רבא praised the fruit of הרפניא.
steps.simpleTranslation: In בבל: אביי would praise the fruits of the right bank of the river, and רבא would praise the fruits of הרפניא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a related note. In בבל, two אמוראים each praised the fruit of a different region.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This follows from ריש לקיש's idea that fertile land hints at גן עדן. Within בבל itself, אביי and רבא each point to a different area as the most fruitful. In this way the גמרא hints at which place might be like the entrance to גן עדן.

keyTerms.meaning: The right bank (of the river פרת)

steps.whatToRemember: The entrance to גן עדן is linked to lush, fertile places. ריש לקיש names three, and in בבל אביי and רבא each praise a different fruitful area.

phrases.english: In Bavel: Abaye would praise
the fruits of the right bank of the river,
and Rava would praise the fruits of Harpanya.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After ריש לקיש's list of possible entrances to גן עדן, the גמרא adds its own separate report about בבל (these are not ריש לקיש's words).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In בבל, אביי pointed to the right bank of the river as the most fruitful place, and רבא pointed to הרפניא.

steps.title: Why does the משנה add 'not untied'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה's phrase about two teams of cattle. It asks why the משנה adds 'and not untied' when 'tied' already says that.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And between them there may be a gap the size of two teams of cattle...' This is obvious! Once the תנא taught that the cattle are tied, we already know they are not untied!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה about the boards around a well. It challenges the extra words 'and not untied,' because they seem to repeat what was already said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה measures the allowed gap by two teams of cattle that are 'tied, and not untied.' The גמרא argues that 'tied' already means 'not untied,' so the second phrase looks extra. This is a challenge to the wording of the משנה. It is not a challenge to the law itself.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious. The גמרא uses this to ask why something needed to be said at all.
Tied. The cattle are bound close together in their team.
Untied, loose. Here it does not mean 'permitted.'
As much as, the full size of.

steps.confusionAlert: Here מוּתָּרוֹת means 'untied/loose.' It does NOT mean 'permitted,' the way it usually does elsewhere.

phrases.english: 'And between them, the size of two [teams of cattle]...' etc.
phrases.notes: A quote from the משנה about the gaps between the boards around a well.

phrases.english: It is obvious!
Since he (the תנא) taught that they are tied,
we already know that they are not untied!

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּשִׁיטָא, כֵּיוָן דִּתְנָא לֵיהּ דִּקְשׁוּרוֹת הָווּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the side discussion about גן עדן and the fruit of בבל, and goes back to the משנה about פסי ביראות.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's extra words 'and not untied.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Tied' already means 'not untied,' so saying both is repetition.

steps.title: 'Tied' means really tied, not just close together
steps.stepSummary: The extra words teach that the cattle must actually be tied. It is not enough for them to stand close together as if they were tied.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have thought that 'tied' only means 'like tied,' standing close together, but not really tied. So the משנה teaches us 'and not untied.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. Without the extra words, we might have read 'tied' loosely, so the משנה spells it out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before the answer, we might think 'tied' just means cattle walking close to each other. The words 'and not untied' tell us they must truly be bound together. That makes the measurement tighter and narrower. The extra phrase is not wasted. It sets the exact width.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said. It introduces a mistaken idea that the text is meant to rule out.

phrases.english: You might have said:
'Tied' means similar to tied (close together),
but not actually tied.
So it teaches us: 'and not untied.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why the extra words are needed. They block a loose reading of 'tied.'
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Tied' might only mean standing close together, like a tied team.
steps.terutzMaskana: The cattle must be truly tied, which gives a narrower measurement.

steps.title: 'One entering and one leaving' means whole teams
steps.stepSummary: A תנא explains that the משנה's 'one entering and one leaving' refers to whole teams of cattle, not single animals.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'One enters and one leaves.' A תנא taught: one team (רבקה) enters and one team leaves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next phrase of the משנה. It brings a teaching that explains exactly what 'one' means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's word 'one' could be read as one single cow. The תנא makes clear that it means one full team of four cattle. So the gap must be wide enough for two whole teams to pass each other.

keyTerms.meaning: A team of cattle. Here it means four animals tied together.

phrases.english: 'One enters and one leaves.'
phrases.notes: A quote from the משנה.

phrases.english: It was taught:
One team enters and one team leaves.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next phrase of the same משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'One' in the משנה means a full team of cattle (רבקה), not a single animal.

steps.title: How big is a cow? The ברייתא's measurements
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא gives a cow's size: its head and most of its body are two אמות long, and it is one and two-thirds אמות thick.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבנן taught: How long are the head and most of the body of a cow? Two אמות. And how thick is a cow? One אמה and two-thirds of an אמה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that gives a cow's measurements. These numbers set up the calculation of the full gap allowed between the boards, and the ברייתא continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To turn 'two teams of cattle' into a real number of אמות, we need the size of one cow. The ברייתא gives two sizes: a length of two אמות and a thickness of one and two-thirds אמות. Only 'head and most of the body' is counted, probably because tied cattle overlap. These numbers will be used to work out the total width.

keyTerms.meaning: Its head and most of its body.

steps.whyThisMatters: These measurements are the building blocks for working out the largest gap allowed between the פסי ביראות.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
How much are the head and most of the body of a cow?
Two cubits.
And how much is the thickness of a cow?
A cubit and two-thirds of a cubit.
phrases.notes: The ברייתא continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: כַּמָּה רֹאשָׁהּ וְרוּבָּהּ שֶׁל פָּרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the team explanation in step 33 by giving the size of each animal, so the gap can be calculated.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A cow's head and most of its body equal 2 אמות. Its thickness equals 1⅔ אמות.
